newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: EU, U.S. advance to ITA pact, world argues on labour.
newsitem.headline: EU, U.S. advance to ITA pact, world argues on labour.

text.p: Hard-won agreement between the United States and Europe on a lucrative pact to free trade in computer technology paved the way on Thursday for a successful inaugural meeting of the world's governing trade body.

However, wrangling among trade ministers over whether to link trade to labour standards and to further liberalise agriculture markets threatened a final declaration that must be finished by the close of the World Trade Organisation (WTO) meeting on Friday.

Europe announced agreement with the United States to scrap tariffs on billions of dollars of information technology trade by the year 2000 and hailed the pact as one of the biggest steps toward global free commerce.

"The basis of what we have agreed with the United States provides for a deal on ITA (information technology agreement) which will be a huge advance for the world economy," European Trade Commissioner Sir Leon Brittan told a news conference.
The Big Four trade powers -- the United States, Japan, the European Union and Canada -- had set the pact as a key target to declaring the WTO's first ministerial meeting a real success.

The breakthrough came when Brittan won endorsement from the 15-member European Union Council for an outline agreement hammered out with the United States in three days of intense, late-night talks at the December 9-13 WTO meeting in Singapore.
The council met after an early morning briefing between Brittan and Acting U.S. trade representative Charlene Barshefsky.
Barshefksy had earlier expressed doubts about European commitment to the ITA accord.

The council mandated Brittan to seek broader support from other countries, many of them Asia's booming tiger economies, for the pact to eliminate worldwide tariffs in the $600 billion infotech sector by the turn of the century.

"This is the biggest trade step forward, if it is completed today, that has happened since the end of the Uruguay Round," Brittan said, referring to the largest set of measures ever adopted to liberalise world trade and completed in 1993.
Brittan said the final agreement still depended on enough countries -- those representing about 90 percent of world trade in the sector -- joining the pact by March 15, 1997.

"Clearly, both Europe and the United States made it clear that this is not a bilateral agreement. It's meant to be agreement covering the countries in the world most involved in this whole area of activity," Brittan said.
Brittan said the 90 percent was not "a rigid barrier", although U.S. officials stressed that it was essential.
"Now the critical objective is to meet the 90 percent product coverage threshold, because if we don't do that the agreement doesn't take effect," Ziegler said.
Some Asian members have already indicated support for the deal, but want flexibility over the timing of the tariff cuts.

Compromise between the United States and the EU had resulted in a deal that would cover the bulk of industrial information technology products, as well as digital photocopiers and capacitors -- circuits used in electronic equipment-- while excluding consumer electronics and audio materials.
The United States, whose high-tech firms would likely profit most has taken the lead in the push to forge a pact. Japan, also a huge player in the fast-growing sector, has backed the drive.

Differences over the contentious issues of discussion in the WTO of competition and investment policies and the way national authorities award contracts, or government procurement, had been resolved, officials said.
"Whoever would have said a week ago we would have agreement there?" said one senior diplomat.

However, a battle on agriculture and linking trade to core labour standards that is seen by many developing countries as a U.S.-backed protectionist ploy were still giving rise to fierce exchanges and holding up the final declaration, delegates said.
A morning meeting broke up without agreement and with India said to be taking the toughest stand.
Asked to describe the talks, Brittan said: "Complicated".

A developing country diplomat closely involved in the effort to find compromise language for the declaration text said: "It's still very confused and very unclear what might come out. Last night it seemed as though we were sinking into quicksand."
However, WTO director general Renato Ruggiero remained upbeat. "The discussion is continuing but the atmosphere is good," he said.
